common_name: Crowborough Calla Lily (Extra-Hardy White Arum Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in early spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Crowborough is one of the hardiest named calla selections, with rhizomes surviving winter in the ground as far north as zone 7 when mulched.

directions: Plant rhizomes in moist to wet, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this selection consistently damp conditions through the growing season. Crowborough is a long-cultivated, RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of the common calla lily prized for flowering earlier and more freely than the species, producing pure white, funnel-shaped spathes above glossy, arrow-shaped green leaves from late spring into summer. It is noted for exceptional winter hardiness among calla lilies, tolerating heavier, wetter soils and colder winters than the tropical hybrid callas, and can be left undisturbed for years where marginal hardy. Where winters are colder than zone 7, mulch heavily in fall or lift and store rhizomes indoors like dahlias; divide congested clumps in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Royal Standard Red Hot Poker (Classic Red and Yellow Torch Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Standard is a long-established Victorian-era cultivar, still one of the most widely grown bicolor red hot pokers.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, taking care that the crown never sits in standing winter moisture, which quickly causes rot. Royal Standard is a classic bicolor selection dating to the 1890s, bearing dense, torch-shaped spikes whose lower florets open bright yellow while the upper buds remain vivid scarlet-red, creating the vivid two-tone effect that gave the genus its common name of red hot poker. It blooms over a long stretch of summer above coarse, grassy, arching foliage and reliably attracts hummingbirds. In colder parts of its hardiness range, tie the foliage over the crown and mulch heavily before the first hard freeze, and divide overcrowded clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom quality high.

common_name: Sunningdale Yellow Red Hot Poker (Clear Yellow Torch Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sunningdale Yellow holds a pure, clear yellow color without the reddish buds typical of most red hot pokers.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential, especially over winter, since waterlogging around the crown causes rot. Sunningdale Yellow is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection valued for its uniform, clear golden-yellow torch-shaped spikes that lack the red or orange buds seen in most red hot poker cultivars, held on sturdy stems above grassy, arching foliage through summer. It blends easily with hot or cool-colored perennial borders alike and draws hummingbirds throughout its long bloom season. Protect the crown with a dry winter mulch in colder parts of its range, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to renew vigor and flowering.

common_name: Corymbose Freesia (Pale Yellow Wild Ancestor Freesia)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free areas (zones 9-10) or start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost in cold climates; a wild South African species used in the early breeding of hybrid freesias.

directions: Plant corms 2 inches deep and 2-3 inches apart in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this Cape species resents wet conditions once it goes dormant after bloom. Freesia corymbosa carries small, fragrant, pale creamy-yellow funnel-shaped flowers held in a loose, corymb-like cluster on wiry stems above narrow, sword-shaped foliage, and was among the wild species used to develop the larger-flowered garden freesia hybrids. It flowers in winter to early spring under its native winter-rainfall, summer-dry climate pattern, so it should be kept dry through summer dormancy. In frost-free gardens the corms are perennial and multiply readily; in colder climates lift after foliage yellows, dry thoroughly, and store in a cool, dry place until fall replanting.

common_name: Rose Queen Corn Lily (Deep Pink Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun. Rose Queen is a long-grown Dutch hybrid corn lily bearing wiry, grass-like stems topped with clusters of star-shaped flowers in a clear deep rose-pink, often with a small darker eye at the center, opening in late spring above slender, sword-shaped foliage. Like other Ixia hybrids, the flowers close on cloudy days and open fully only in bright sun, so plant in the sunniest available spot and in generous drifts for the best display. Allow foliage to die back completely after bloom before removing it, and in climates with wet summers, lift corms and store dry until fall to prevent rot during dormancy.

common_name: Vulcan Corn Lily (Fiery Red-Orange Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun. Vulcan is a classic Dutch hybrid corn lily producing wiry stems set with star-shaped flowers in a vivid fiery red-orange, each with a small dark central eye, opening in late spring above slender, grass-like foliage. As with other Ixia hybrids the blooms stay closed in overcast weather and open only in strong sunlight, so a full-sun site is essential for a good show, and plants look best massed in groups of 25 or more. Let the foliage yellow and die back naturally after flowering before cutting it away, and in regions with humid or wet summers, lift the corms and store them dry until fall to avoid rot during the required dry dormancy.
